China's space programme is run by the China National Space Administration (CNSA), founded 22 April 1993, headquartered in Haidian District, Beijing.
Tiangong ('Heavenly Palace') is China's modular space station. Its core module Tianhe launched 29 April 2021; Wentian and Mengtian followed in 2022. It orbits Earth at roughly 340-450 km.
Tiangong supports a permanent crew of three (six during handovers), making it the third long-duration crewed station in history after Mir and the ISS.
BeiDou is China's global navigation satellite system. Phase-3 completed in June 2020 with a 35-satellite constellation across MEO, IGSO and GEO orbits.
China became the third country to put a human in space — Yang Liwei flew aboard Shenzhou 5 on 15 October 2003, joining Russia (1961) and the United States (1962).
China's four orbital launch sites: Jiuquan (JSLC, inland Gobi), Xichang (XSLC, Sichuan), Taiyuan (TSLC, Shanxi) and Wenchang (Hainan island, opened 2014 and the only coastal site).

Long March 5 (CZ-5) is China's heaviest operational rocket — about 25 t to low-Earth orbit and 14 t to geostationary transfer. It enabled the Tianhe station module and the Chang'e lunar return missions.
Chang'e 5 (Dec 2020) was the first lunar sample-return mission since the Soviet Luna 24 in 1976, bringing back roughly 1.7 kg of lunar material.
China's Mars rover Zhurong landed in Utopia Planitia on 14 May 2021, making China the second country after the United States to operate a rover on Mars.
China launched the world's first quantum-communications satellite, Mozi (QUESS), on 16 August 2016. It demonstrated entanglement-based key distribution over more than 1 200 km.
Yaogan is China's reconnaissance / ISR constellation. By 2024 it had grown past 100 active satellites — the world's largest dedicated military ISR fleet.

Gaofen ('High Resolution') is China's civilian Earth-observation series under the CHEOS programme. Gaofen-4 is in geostationary orbit, giving continuous 50-metre-visible / 400-metre-IR coverage of Asia.
FengYun (风云, 'Wind & Cloud') is China's weather-satellite series, run by the CMA. Polar-orbit Fengyuns (FY-3, FY-5) and geostationary Fengyuns (FY-2, FY-4) operate side by side.
Hongyan and Guowang are China's planned LEO broadband megaconstellations. Guowang alone plans about 13 000 satellites to compete with Starlink.
Tiangong is visible to the naked eye when it passes overhead at night, transiting with a magnitude roughly similar to Venus.
China launched the Einstein Probe X-ray observatory on 9 January 2024 — its lobster-eye optics give it the widest soft-X-ray field of view of any space telescope.

China became the first country to soft-land on the far side of the Moon when Chang'e 4 touched down in the Von Kármán crater on 3 January 2019, paired with the Queqiao relay satellite at the Earth-Moon L2 point.
Tianlian (天链) is China's geostationary data-relay constellation — the Chinese equivalent of NASA's TDRSS, providing high-bandwidth space-to-ground links for crewed and Earth-observation missions.
Beijing's commercial new-space sector has launched several small-payload rockets: LandSpace's Zhuque-2 was the first methalox rocket worldwide to reach orbit (12 July 2023).
Shijian (实践, 'Practice') is China's experimental / technology-demonstration line. Many Shijian satellites carry rendezvous and proximity-operations payloads of strategic interest.
